newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hong Kong may adopt some human rights laws - China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong may adopt some human rights laws - China.

text.p: Chinese-run Hong Kong might consider adopting international human rights laws if these regulations are "the same" as the communist country's laws, a senior Chinese official said on Saturday.
The official also said the running of Hong Kong should not be debated internationally, saying such a move would only raise fears among the business community and hurt investment.

"International laws are different from China's domestic laws and if we want to adopt international laws, they must be the same as China's domestic laws," Guo Chongli, spokesman for China's delegation to a meeting of European and Asian foreign ministers in Singapore, told journalists.
But he said if international laws and Chinese laws were compatible, they could be adopted.
"We need time to study this," Guo said when asked whether such studies would be completed before the handover of Hong Kong to China from Britain at midnight on June 30.
"Legal experts need to make in-depth studies...It is too early to discuss this now," he added.
Britain, the current Hong Kong authorities, and a number of Western countries have expressed concern over the future of human rights in the territory after the handover.

On Friday, Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and his British counterpart Malcolm Rifkind met but failed to reach ageement on a provisional legislature established by Beijing to set laws for the territory after the handover.
"The issue (of Hong Kong) should be handled by China and Britain together but after June 30, it will be China's internal affair," Guo said.

Britain has complained the provisional legislature breaks previous promises made by Beijing over the post-handover Hong Kong constitution, and has suggested the issue be raised at the International Court of Justice (world court) in the Hague.

Britain has also said it is keen to raise the international profile of civil rights issues in Hong Kong, hoping this will increase pressure on Beijing to respect the wishes of the territory's 6.3 million people.
"The higher the profile of these issues, the higher the price China will have to pay for changing Hong Kong," one senior British official told reporters.
But Guo said an international debate over Hong Kong could merely damage its business prospects.
"If you internationalise the Hong Kong issue, it would trigger doubts among foreign businessmen and hurt their investment willingness and that is bad for Hong Kong," Guo said.
"Not necessarily Britain, but some people may be happy to see this. Hong Kong people should have clear understanding about the fact," he said without elaboration.
He said China did not want Hong Kong discussed at Saturday's ministerial meeting in Singapore.
"I don't think the Hong Kong issue should be on the agenda of today's meeting. It is not right to discuss this issue in this international occasion," Guo said.
